utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Is everybody ready. Does everybody hear? The Prosecutor, my colleagues, the Defence, General Blaskic, do you hear me? Very well. Mr. Prosecutor, perhaps we might resume now, or do you have a motion you would like to present first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, your Honours, good morning, counsel. Mr. President, I have a rather sensitive issue I would like to raise with the court in closed session, private session; if I could do that either before or after the witness testifies I would greatly appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will take up the question immediately. Let us move into a closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, do you think that we might conclude by around 1.00 or 1.15, does that seem possible to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is possible, Mr. President. I am not sure how this witness is going to do. He is an elderly gentleman, as you know it is difficult to know how quickly they will move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. This is not a protected witness, if I am not mistaken. Who are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I would like to bring that to your Honours' attention. He was going to be a protected witness and literally at the break this morning he decided he did not want protection. The gentleman's name is Ibrahim Nuhagic, that is I-B-R-A-H-I-M, last name N-U-H-A-G-I-C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Ibrahim, Nuhagic, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, consistent with the prior presentations by the Office of the Prosecutor concerning the relevance of the testimony, we will once again be moving to another village and this is the village of Ocehnice, as your Honours can see in counts 2 and 4 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is the name of the village again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ocehnice. It is on page 7 of the indictment. It is O-C-E-H-N-I-C-E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Page 7 of the indictment in the French version, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you are right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Likewise in counts 11 and 13 and hopefully it is page 9 in the French version as well, relating to the destruction and plunder of property, the village is named there as well. In this particular aspect, we will, as I said at the outset, move into the municipality of Busovaca, following along on the testimony that the Chamber heard concerning the village of Loncari. This witness will talk about the events that began in the municipality of Busovaca in January 1993, where the HVO came to their village in late January, incarcerated the men at the Kaonik Prison, beat them along the way, took them to dig trenches for a significant period of time. Some of the Bosnian Muslim men taken to dig those trenches were in fact killed. They were released in February with the assistance of the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: July 1993, you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: January 1993, Mr. President. After this witness and the other Bosnian men were released, they were then attacked on 19th April 1993, this witness's village, the village of Ocehnice was burnt to the ground. His mother, his wife, his sister and his two nieces were machine-gunned to death. He escaped with several other individuals in the village. He then, after being questioned on one occasion by the police, moved into a relative's house in Busovaca. Shortly after that, approximately 30 days, the Muslim residents of that house were thrown out, the house was occupied by Bosnian Croats; they went to a second house, they were thrown out of that house. Then they went to a third house and they were thrown out of that house, all by the HVO. They were then taken to a village called Skradno and the village Skradno is in the area between Vitez and Busovaca. Skradno was a village and essentially they were in custody and prevented from moving in Skradno and from Skradno the HVO took them to dig trenches over a period of time in and around the Skradno area, specifically on the front-lines in Kula. He will talk about having seen the accused along with Kordic, Kostroman and Valenta frequently on television. He will talk about an individual who we have not introduced to date, by the name of Zoran Maric. Zoran Maric was the President of the Busovaca municipality. He will talk about a particular speech that Maric gave at a rally which the accused attended. Finally he will talk about an individual who is a member of the Jokers who gave an interview to the media that he observed concerning the excellent job that the HVO troops did in the village of Loncari. All of the items I have addressed, Mr. President and your Honours, deal with the counts on the indictment, specifically 2 and 4, directly counts 5 and 10, count 11 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. You are going a little fast. I know we have to go fast, but let me try to follow you here. Two to 4, paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Counts 5 to 10 and counts 11 through 13, and all of the evidence, Mr. President, goes to count 1, which is the persecution count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am not doing this just for the sake of doing it, you understand that the judges want to be sure that in the questions you ask, the facts are illustrated in light of the charges that you brought against the General. Very well, you may have the accused brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: How old is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At this juncture, Mr. President, he is approaching his 63rd birthday. He was born on 10th January 1935.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You think that is old? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is not old by our standards, Mr. President, but I think that people age a little more quickly in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you hear me? Please stand up. Please stand. Thank you. Please tell the Tribunal -- have no fears, rest assured, tell us your name and your first name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ibrahim Nuhagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please remain standing, and the usher is going to give you a solemn declaration which you will be asked to read in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I do it out loud or shall I just read it to myself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Read it out loud, please. It is an oath that you are taking. MR. IBRAHIM NUHAGIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nuhagic. You may be seated. The Prosecutor -- do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have agreed to come to testify before this Tribunal, and the Tribunal thanks you for doing so. You may speak without fear, you are before judges who will listen to you, of course, ask you questions, the Prosecutor will ask you questions and then the Defence attorneys will also ask you questions. The Prosecutor has told us briefly which events you were witness to and which you experienced and which through you suffered. Speak to us specifically first of all of the events of January 1993 at the time that the HVO came and committed a certain number of acts against you. Then we will speak about the events of April 1993, the attack on your village, the fires. Perhaps you might even speak to us, even though it would be very painful, of the death of people close to you, deaths under difficult conditions, and then this long flight through several villages. These are the essential points which the Tribunal would like to hear you speak about. The Tribunal will occasionally ask you some questions. Have no fears, and then he will specify certain points in light of the serious charges that have been brought against General Blaskic. Mr. Kehoe, perhaps you have some preliminary, general type of questions to ask before the witness makes his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. President, thank you. Good morning, Mr. Nuhagic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, can you tell the court how old you are at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, are you a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, prior to 19th April 1993, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the village of Ocehnice, in the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, beginning in January 1993, and if we can extend this through your period of time in Skradno in September 1993, can you tell the judges what happened to you and your family, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I start with 1993, April 1993 or January of 1993, when we were taken to prison?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: January 1993, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In January 1993, at night, it was dusk, the HVO soldiers came to the village. They rounded up myself and my neighbours. We had some weapons from before which we shared with the HVO in 1992 and 1993, in the beginning, and on 27th January, they rounded us up, both us and the weapons, and we had to keep our hands behind our heads all the time, all the way to the camp. On the way, they abused us, there were blows up until we came down to the road. As we were entering the bus, there was a cordon of these soldiers, and we passed through this gauntlet. Nobody could pass without receiving a blow, in whichever part of the body it came. From there, the bus started in the direction of Busovaca. It came to stop in the bus station in Busovaca, an auxiliary platform, and then they ordered us out of the bus, and to turn and face the wall of the bus station. Then a van arrived which had a four-barrel anti-aircraft gun on it. When this vehicle stopped, came to a stop near us, the crew dismounted the vehicle and started hitting us there, and I received the most blows in my back. I still suffer consequences of that. Meanwhile, one of the HVO soldiers objected to this, why they were beating us. They started arguing over this among themselves, so that they stopped beating us. Then they again ordered us in the bus, and the bus went along the road towards the blue 11. When we came to -- there was a unit whose commander was Mladen Agatic, and his deputy was Ivan Akrap. Again, as we got off the bus, they kept beating us all the way until we entered the building. In there, there was a lot of mistreatment and acts of provocation, and among -- the person that I noticed the most there was Ivan Popovic. He was the most prominent among them in this. We spent some time there, and the order again came for us to get back on to the bus. There again a gauntlet, a cordon on the way to the bus and again nobody could escape blows. Fehim, nicknamed Borovo was singled out. When they got him off the bus, they beat him a lot. He was trying to get on to the bus away from them, but Ivan Akrap prevented him, and he said that he was now in command there. When this beating was finished and he had entered the bus, we came to the Kaonik camp. In Kaonik, we gave our first and last names, and we were put in the improvised cells. Other cells were filled with prisoners who were all of Muslim ethnic background. We could not all fit in one cell, so we were all together six and so we were put into three separate cells, one in one, two in another and three in another. I was feeling the blows that I had received a lot and I could not sleep that night, and I asked to be seen by the doctor that they had. They took me to their physician, but I could not stay in the room with him by myself, there was a HVO soldier who had escorted me there, he stayed in the room. I could not say that I was hit by the HVO soldiers, but instead I lied that I had fallen off the barn as I was feeding my livestock on that day when I was detained. It was very tight there in those, they were small cells and we were many. There were some boards there only, which were laid down in these cells. There was some hay, some dried grass that was thrown on top of it. There was some clothing from the former JNA, there were some coats and some blankets, things like that. The conditions were very poor. There was only one toilet for 400 or maybe 500 people, so if somebody needed to go and relieve himself, they took us out, and we were surrounded with these HVO soldiers who carried weapons so that someone would not try to flee, and then they would be taken back to the cells in the camp and were told that nobody was to ask to be taken out in another hour or two. The food was very bad and there was very little of it. The portions that we were getting would not have been enough for one person, and we had to split that portion in two. The utensils were not washed, the cutlery. One group would leave and the next group would arrive at the same table and the food would be just poured into those same plates. People were taken out to dig trenches. I did not go to dig trenches. The doctor gave me a certificate and some pills for my pains, so that I would not be forced to go to dig. Since I could not sleep and there were even no conditions for it, I could not lie down anywhere. I was in pains and at night, we could hear moans in the -- some of the soldiers would take people out from the cells and they would beat them and mistreat them. They were asking for money, watches, valuables that people had on them. We could not keep those things, we could not protect them. We had to give them away. The Red Cross came and they registered us, and the people who went to dig complained that they were being treated poorly, that the soldiers who were guarding them were beating them, and were even ordering that they beat one another. They did not want to hit each other hard, and that soldier takes that same shovel and then he would tell the two who were supposed to hit each other how to hit each other, he would demonstrate it for them. There were some people who even succumbed from all the beating they received during the digging. I remember well Mustafa Ibragic, whose nickname was Cakara. He was beaten up and he was tied to a vehicle. He came back to the Kaonik camp with the rest of them who went out digging, his comrades from the cell asked for help so that Mustafa Ibragic would be given some medical help. Apparently they took him out of the cell but no one knows where they took him and how it went. He was returned to the cell and in the cell he died. I also heard of two others, whose names I do not know. We were there until February, and then we were let go, we were allowed to go back home and most of us decided to return to our homes. We were told that nobody would bother us. Until April 1993, it was like that and so we even started to work on our fields. Some time in the afternoon, the HVO soldiers simply walked in the village. We had nothing at that time and there was nobody to put up any resistance and we could not do anything, because we were under the HVO control. They started burning and killing whoever they could reach. At the time I was in the outhouse and I was able to escape and save myself. They noticed as I was fleeing and they shot after me, but fortunately I was not hit by any bullets. As I was fleeing away from the house, there was about 50 metres of a clearing, I was going zigzig, and I jumped into some kind of a trash heap, and the soldiers who were shooting after me, I think, reckoned that they had shot me down. I waited there for a while, I could not hear any footsteps in the vicinity, and after a while, I even raised my head a little bit, so that I could see what was going on in the village, what was all that heavy shooting about. As I looked up, I saw that my barn was on fire. Then I came to understand what it was about. I had to wait a little bit more and I had to hide a bit better. I could hear as the glass was shattering in the houses in the village, so that more air would come in and so that the house would burn better. When my uncle heard the shooting in the village, he came out of the house to see what was going on. He saw the smoke coming out of my barn, he saw that the barn was on fire. He tried to go in and let the livestock out, but he did not manage to get there, because he was noticed by a soldier from my yard and this soldier shot at him and wounded him. He pulled back, there was a cellar in the house where the food was kept over the winter, he fled into that cellar where there were other villagers, neighbours of his and mine. They were searching the houses, they went looking to the upper floors. They did not find anyone, they were yelling, "where is the old man, where did he hide?". They continued doing what they were doing in the village, that is setting the houses on fire, breaking windows, and my family, who attempted to leave the ground floor, did not succeed in doing so. The HVO soldiers killed them in front of the house at the doorstep. The roof construction was collapsing as the house was burning. I saw when it grew dark that the soldiers were no longer around, they had finished their job. I came back to my house and circled it. I saw that my mother was on fire, and my wife. I managed to put out the fire on them, and my uncle who was wounded came over to me down the road and he said, "Ibrahim, take care of yourself. We cannot save what is gone, but we have to think of ourselves". That is what I did with my uncle and some other neighbours, we got together that evening, and we went to Busovaca through the woods. We hid and we went very silently, so that nothing could surprise us. We reached Busovaca. My uncle and I decided to go and stay with my uncle's son. In the meantime, I was not feeling comfortable about my dear ones lying there unburied in the village, so I decided to go to the Dzemat committee, which is the Islamic association in Busovaca, to ask them whether they could do anything through the Red Cross or the UNPROFOR to ask permission for burial. In the meantime, the HVO police learnt that I was there, and that I was a living witness of what had been done in the village, because the group that was doing this in the village had told their command that no one in the village had survived the operation. When they arrested me and took me to the HVO police station, I saw bloodstains on the floor and on the walls. They took me inside for interrogation. Then I was subjected to mistreatment, threats, and I myself felt scared, seeing where I was. During the interrogation itself, they tried in various ways to trick me into saying that the HVO had killed the people and burnt the village. I did not agree to those traps of theirs. Then they asked how come I had survived when my closest relatives had died. I lied, and I said that I was in a shelter with some other neighbours. Then this same interrogator cursed my balija God, and said, "where are those neighbours, then?" I said that we had together come down to Busovaca that evening. He asked me, "how many were you?"; I could not remember straight away before I started listing the names. When I listed the names, there were 11 of us, 11 persons. Then he realised I was not alone, so he told me that I would go to a cell next to the entrance downstairs, and I was kept in that cell for a time while they were checking whether I had told the truth when I had said there were 11 of us who had come down. When they had verified my story, and when they saw that it was true, then they asked me, "how come the whole village was burnt down?". Then I thought to myself, what am I going to say? I cannot say that they had done it. So I lied again, and said it was enough for one or two houses to start burning, and he asked, "was there any shelling there?"; I lied and said there was. I was afraid for my life, I did not dare say that they had done it. He asked me, where did they come from and I said I did not know because I was in a shelter at my other neighbour's, but they kept insisting that I should admit that they were the ones who had done it. So I said, you know that the village has wooden barns, wooden fences linked together, so it would be enough to set fire to one or two houses for all of them to catch fire in this dry weather. Then they shut me up again in the cell, and leaving the police station, after the interrogation, the soldiers were there at the door asking, "did they ask about us?". When we came out, they asked the interrogator whether I had told about them, and the interrogator said that I had not. Then he told me that he would keep me in the cell for a while until he decided what to do with me. It was night-time, I do not know exactly what time it was, it seemed a long time to me, because I was terribly afraid, because I was listening. This was the HVO station that was on duty, and I heard Mato Ninic, who was formerly a member of the police, and he was on duty in the police station that night, and there were some others, young soldiers passing by who were full of themselves. They were using various threats, they were singing all kinds of songs, all kinds of goings-on. I was simply waiting when my turn would come. In the meantime, the door opened and he told me to come out, a policeman told me, a policeman I knew. I looked at him to see whether I could recognise him and I did. His name is Marijan Varesak. He asked me where I was going to sleep. I was astonished by his question. Was this a lie or was it true? He said, "calm down, everything has ended well". I said I did not know where I should go, because I had been taken into custody at my cousin's, Saban. They took me to the house, and the same man told me not to move anywhere, not to go anywhere, to stay there at my relative's. So I stayed there about a month at my relative's, with my uncle. One evening, HVO soldiers came. They kept asking whether we had any radio stations or weapons. How could we have any of those things when we were in their hands, the HVO had control of this area, so it was impossible. But they kept pressuring us so much and hitting us, and they would say that there was someone who knows that my relative Saban had this, but he could not confess, since he did not have it. They took Edo Hidarovic back from the camp, where they had taken him three hours before they came to visit us. They had beaten him up and he had to confess and he was lying on the steps of Saban's building. He was the one who had confessed that Saban had this. He did have a hunting rifle, but that had been seized from him earlier on as it had from all the rest of us already in January. But this was an excuse for them to throw us out of the house. That evening, we were thrown out, myself, my uncle and Saban. They did not care where we would go, they just said we had to leave, and so we had no other way but to go and find accommodation elsewhere with another relative. That evening, when I was thrown out of Saban's house, I recognised Zlatko Aleksovski, who was the prison warden. There were two small police cars, and in front of them was a van as the third vehicle. Zlatko Aleksovski asked me how old I was. I lied then, I said I was older than I was, over 60, because I was afraid that I would be taken to prison, together with Saban. He said we had to go wherever we wanted, but as long as we would not still be on the road, so we did. There was a fence and we quickly entered the yard of another relative called Mustafa on the other side of the road. We spent a night there at our relative Mustafa's. Then the soldiers, or rather the HVO police, came again, and they threw us out of that house too, Mustafa's house. Then another relative, Hazim, and again they rounded us all up from Hazim's house and took us to the village of Skradno. This village of Skradno was some kind of a collection centre, and it was also under the HVO control. In that village, there were two HVO soldiers on patrol. I know one of them, Pero Sapic, who was a member of the patrol, and I stayed in Skradno until the end of September. In September, there was an illegal exchange. Apparently, it was done in secret, so that not even the police or the HVO or anyone knew about it. This was carried out by soldiers from Zenica, the Zenica municipality, and I do not know who else who came to Busovaca, and their families stayed behind in Zenica and the villages around Zenica. So I know Darko Arapovic, who helped us get out of the village of Skradno. Then the family of one of the HVO soldiers from Zenica had to come here, for example, and I would go there. I was staying with Atif Barucija and then Darko gave him an address in Zenica municipality, telling him which families need to come over, and until Atif brought those families over, we could not go. I myself, his mother and his wife. That is how it was done, so that the whole village left, and in Skradno, 90 per cent of the people were exiled from Busovaca, people whom they had chased out of their homes and brought to Skradno. I saw that there were people from Jajce there too, who first stopped in Vitez and then they were chased out of there and brought to Skradno. There were people from Vitez too, from the village of Loncari there were people, but all of them were illegally exchanged, illegally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you have any additional questions for the witness, something that the witness has not told us in connection with the events? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, can you tell the judges how big a village Ocehnice was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a village with about eight houses, maybe nine families were living in the village. It was not a large village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did the village include just Muslims or did it have Muslim and Croats in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just Muslims, and on the other side was also Ocehnice, but they were Croats. They were there until 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, in January, when you said the soldiers had come to your village on 27th January and took the men, were these HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see how they were dressed and did you see them with any HVO insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was night-time, they had masks over their faces. The two of those I recognised by the way they spoke among the group that attacked us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now you also mentioned that on the way down to the bus, all of the men were beat and then you had to walk through a column of soldiers and you were beat again then, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were all of the victims of those beatings Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You mentioned that you also got off the bus when you came across a truck with an anti-aircraft weapon on it and the soldiers got off of the truck and beat the people on the bus, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was when I was beaten the worst.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Nuhagic, were the soldiers that did the beating HVO soldiers and were the victims Muslim men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you were taken on the bus and taken into Busovaca, did you come in contact with Ivan Papovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not Papovic, I do not understand the name Papovic. Perhaps Popovic Ivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Did you come across Popovic Ivan? Was he an HVO soldier and did he abuse you in any way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the "11 Blue" in Donje Polje, "Jedanest Plavih".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did he do to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He made up various things, saying that we were balijas, that we all need to be got rid of, all the worst possible things he could think of. Allegedly, he did not have a knife on him, and he sent the soldiers to go and fetch a knife. We expected him to get hold of a knife and do who knows what, but in the meantime, the bus came, but we had to pass between these two columns and be beaten. There was no way we could avoid it. He was in the bus too, as far as Kaonik. He was saying various things and mistreating people, I know he beat Hamdija Lusija, and he asked him for his brother, Hamdija's brother, where he was and he answered he did not know, and he did not. He would frequently come to the camp and mistreat people, open the cells and threaten them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, at some point did someone search you and take a calendar away from you and force you to eat that calendar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this same person, Ivan Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Why did he force you to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because it had the symbols of Bosnia-Herzegovina on it. I had to eat it, because he was ready to beat me up and out of fear, I had to eat it and I must apologise, but I wet my pants in the process, because he was getting ready to beat me up. So I had to swallow. I was forced to swallow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Moving ahead to your time when you were imprisoned in Kaonik Prison and you said there were between 400 and 500 prisoners in the camp. Were they all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How many people were there, how many men were there in each cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depended. In some cases, up to 25, in others 18. It depended how many people could be crammed in. They did not care, nobody could lie down, we had to sit in the cells, because they were overcrowded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were put in cells. Were these cells newly built, Mr. Nuhagic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- yes, they were improvised. They had not even been completed. This was the warehouse of the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did it appear to you, Mr. Nuhagic, that they were planning for all of you prisoners to be incarcerated in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At first, we thought we would be kept there all the time, and the camp was intended for Central Bosnia. But it had not been completed, it was terrible, it was intolerable there. There was no heating, there was nothing. The cells were overflowing, and then in another warehouse, there were no wooden boards or anything. When they brought in people from the village of Skradno to this other warehouse, and I was taken there too when they took me out of the cells, only the working groups allegedly stayed on, whereas those of us who were not capable of working were taken to this other ordinary depot where it was really intolerable. They told us that we should find a pallet outside, a pile of bricks or anything we could find outside, and they gave us one blanket each. So I spent several days there in this empty warehouse. It was cold, it was January/February, you know how cold it gets in Bosnia in those days, and especially since I had suffered such terrible blows.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, you said that individuals were taken out to dig trenches, that Bosnian Muslim men were taken out to dig trenches. How many were taken out to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not have figured it out, but I could hear them calling them out in the hallway. A lot of them went, because when they were arriving in the camp, their names and their birth dates were taken down, and in the morning, when the time came to go to work, the soldier in charge would yell loudly in the hallway that everybody should listen to the names being called out, and whoever is called out would have to come out into the hallway. So there would be one group, two groups, however many they would need for the day. For instance, during the day, the cells would be nearly empty, all of them. In the evening, they would return very late, and sometimes some people would not be coming back for several days, no one would see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, you said soldiers would call out names; were these HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the HVO soldiers who were calling people out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know where these individuals were taken to dig trenches in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know, Kula, Bare, Strane, I also heard of a place called Prosje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me move ahead, Mr. Nuhagic. You also mentioned that a man by the name of Mustafa Ibragic died in jail.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was he a Muslim victim as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When the Red Cross came, did the men that were digging the trenches complain to the Red Cross about the digging of trenches and their abuse when they were digging the trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not dare, because the interpreters were also members of the HVO. Only if the Red Cross found someone digging the trenches on their way. This happened to Jasmin Ekmecic. He was in a group that was digging and the UNPROFOR prevented this and the UNPROFOR told them to be taken back to the barracks, but the UNPROFOR was not around every day to see these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: May I just ask, were these trenches on the front-line, could you ask him, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, did you hear Judge Riad's question? Were these trenches on the front-line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the demarcation line, where the HVO held their line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, let us move ahead to April 1993. What was the day that the HVO soldiers came in and burned your village and murdered your loved ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 19th April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: After that event, Mr. Nuhagic, had you heard that the reason for the attack was that the Bosnian army had shelled the Draga barracks? Had you heard that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that from stories, that that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Had you also heard that the HVO maintained that the shelling of the Draga barracks came from your village? Had you heard that also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the worst thing, Ivo Kristo, called Cajo, said this. He said that the shells were coming from Nuhagici, from Ocehnice. They could not come from the Nuhagici, from Ocehnice when we were under the HVO control, because in January, three rifles and my hunting rifle were taken away from us at that occasion, and there was none left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So did any shelling from your village, was any shelling taking place in your village directed towards the Draga barracks, or anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Interpretation problem; do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think he put his elbow on the button.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Prosecutor will repeat the question for you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, did any shelling take place from your village towards the Draga barracks at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, when these soldiers came into your village, did you see how they were dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wore masks for the most part. They had like stockings and they had just slits for eyes and mouth, so that we would not recognise them. I could only recognise them by some of their nicknames.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who were the individuals you recognised by their nicknames?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one who was in command were just to say Zare, Zeljo, Cigo, so he was calling them by their nicknames, so that is how he called them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you know if these individuals were members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You mentioned during your narrative, Mr. Nuhagic, that your wife's body was burning and your mother's body was burning. Were any other members of your family murdered that day in the same village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my mother was killed there, my wife, my sister, and two daughters of my brothers who were staying with me in my house. When the soldiers came to do whatever they were going to do there, they all tried to flee, but they were all killed in the yard in front of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you went to look at your wife's body and your mother's body burning, did you see the other three bodies lying there also?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were together and as they were walking one behind the other, they were all one next to another. Had I not put out the fire on my mother, my sister and my two brothers' daughters would also have burned, because they were next to each other as they were falling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So on that day, five members of your family were murdered and every Muslim house in the village was burnt, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, whatever could have burned did burn. Livestock was killed in the barns. One of the soldiers, I am not going to tell his name, he opened one of the barns and let the livestock out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: One of the soldiers tried to protect the livestock, is that right? One of the HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Moving ahead to in Busovaca when you said that you were questioned by the police, and you noted in your narrative that the police tried to get you to say that the HVO did the killing, but you did not want to fall for that trick. Why did you not want to tell them that you saw the HVO commit this attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not dare, because my life was at stake. The HVO soldiers who did this said that they had killed, that they had annihilated everybody in the village and nobody had survived. I was assuming that I was the only witness left, and meanwhile, this interrogation took place as I already described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did you believe was going to happen if you told those police that the HVO had done this attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I would be executed, that I would be killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that the witness has already made that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: These policemen that were in these headquarters, did they have white belts on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see that, they were sitting down at a table. But it was -- they had military uniforms on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, did you also learn that the actual attack on your village was ordered by Pasko Lubacic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned that Pasko Lubacic was the leader of the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Moving ahead on your narrative, Mr. Nuhagic, you said that ultimately you went to your cousin's Saban's house and that you were forced out of that house, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you see who moved into Saban's house after you were forced out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were there two days and when they threw us out, they said, "our guys are going to be stationed here now".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When they said, "our guys", who did you understand them to be talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Meaning the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ultimately you were taken to Skradno. Did the HVO take you to the village of Skradno?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they put us in the truck, myself, my two cousins and their families.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you got to Skradno, were there other -- approximately how many other Muslims were in Skradno?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think that I could say that, but I have heard -- I do not think that one could have estimated. From the Barucijas, my relatives with whom I was staying, I heard there were people from Velika Bukovica, Travnik, that Mijo Batinic brought 97 of them, the elderly, women, children, to the village of Skradno in a truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, you said this was a collection centre; was it patrolled by HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You got there approximately when, in May 1993 and stayed until September 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: During that time, did HVO soldiers come and take Bosnian Muslim men out to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How often did this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They created shifts, they were digging through the night and during the day they would be at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did this continue up until the time you left in September 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Where did these men go to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The one who went to dig at Kula, Strane, Bare.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sir, let me move to some other topics. When you were living in your village in Ocehnice, did you have occasion to watch television frequently and see the accused, Colonel Blaskic, on television with other HVO leaders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those who had any desire could watch the Busovaca television every day, they had programmes between 4.00 and 6.00 every night on HTV.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What HVO leaders did you see on this programme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was known that Dario Kordic was the HVO leader. I also saw Tihomir Blaskic, Ante Valenta, Ignjac Kostroman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What were they talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were talking, this was not on television -- this was at the end for the most part, Kordic would be talking certain things, but I remember very well Ante Valenta. I was not watching this television very much, it was for people who were interested in that, but occasionally I would watch it when I did not have other things to do outdoors. But I do remember very well Ante Valenta when he said that the mujezin, who was talking from the mosque, was bothering him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were these individuals on television frequently together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could show you a photograph and begin with, excuse me, with the assistance of the usher if we could put it on the ELMO, Exhibit 80/9 and then I will move to 80/8.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to put on my glasses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, do you recognise anybody in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ante Stipac; Blaskic, Dario Kordic; Ignjac Kostroman. I cannot see Ante Valenta here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us go to the next photograph, then, the next photograph 80/8. Is Ante Valenta in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, here he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are pointing to Valenta. Do you recognise anybody else in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise Zoran Maric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell us about Zoran Maric. Come back to the microphone Mr. Nuhagic. You are pointing to the man in the middle of the photograph with the beard. Who was Zoran Maric? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zoran Maric was the President of the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you ever see him on TV giving a speech at a rally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the stadium in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did you hear him say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was saying when the soldiers were swearing the oath, he said that in this area only one kind of plant should grow. I could not figure out at that time what it meant, until we figured it out later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did you figure out, Mr. Nuhagic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We saw when this cleansing started, this ethnic cleansing, that Busovaca was to be cleansed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was Blaskic at that rally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Was Blaskic at that rally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Blaskic, Kordic, Tihomir Blaskic that is, Dario Kordic, Ante Valenta, Ignjac Kostroman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Moving ahead to another subject, Mr. Nuhagic, when you were in your cousin's house in Busovaca, did you see a television programme where Mirko Cosic was interviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Who was Mirko Cosic and where was he interviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Busovaca, in the park at the bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What was he? Was he an HVO soldier as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The commander of the unit called Jokers, who wore black uniforms, and they were for special purpose unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, did the interviewer ask Mirko Cosic about what his soldiers had done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was bragging that they were doing a good job for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did he mention the village of Loncari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he first mentioned Kula, Polom, and he was especially satisfied with how they did the job in the village of Loncari. He did not make any additional comments into the camera, but I remember well him saying, "the time will show".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to put just several exhibits into evidence and I will complete my questioning of Mr. Nuhagic. The first exhibit is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is Exhibit 180, it is again a Rule 70 photograph that has been given to the Defence. It is another aerial photograph that has been given to the Office of the Prosecutor under the restrictions of Rule 70. The next exhibit that I would like to move to, Mr. President, is Exhibit 181 and that is a portion of Exhibit 180. If I could put Exhibit 181 on the ELMO so that the witness can identify it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, can you put your glasses on again, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If you can take a look at the exhibit on the ELMO, Exhibit 181, and there are two circles, one numbered 1 and the other numbered 2. What is the number 1, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the former JNA, it is all under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Number 2, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- called Draga, and number 2 is my village. Number 2 is my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Approximately how far is the Draga barracks from the town of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 1 kilometre, maybe 1.5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That would be in the direction of Kiseljak, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could move to the next exhibit with the assistance of the usher, which is Exhibit 182, and again, Mr. President and your Honours, 182 is an enlargement of Exhibit 58. Mr. Nuhagic, this is a photograph that has been in evidence of the Kaonik camp. Do you recognise the actual building that is encircled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What is that building? Is that where you were held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we could move to the last exhibit, Mr. President, which is Exhibit 183, which is an enlargement of Exhibit 29, the map. If I could put Exhibit 183 on the ELMO. Mr. Nuhagic, you see referenced, underlined in yellow, your village Ocehnice, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You also see the area, as you are moving up the page , Kula, and was that one of the areas where the prisoners were digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just going further up the page, the village of Skradno is highlighted, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is where you were being held until September 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Lastly on this map, you see the last highlighting, the notation of Kaonik where the prison was, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nuhagic. Mr. President, I have no further questions, I would just like to move into evidence Exhibits 180 through 183.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, the exhibits will be admitted with the numbers given by the Registrar. You can begin the cross-examination. Is it Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, I wish to consult my colleagues. (Pause). For various reasons, the Trial Chamber will continue with the hearing of the witness until the end of the cross-examination, the re-examination and the questions of the judges. We are just going to have a five or six minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed, please bring in the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First of all, I should like to have the witness brought in. I wish to thank the interpreters for their co-operation. It is a problem relating to security and we thank them and we will finish with the witness this afternoon, so he will not have to come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nuhagic, do you hear me? Are the microphones switched on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have you had a little rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I hope you hear me too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You know that the accused has attorneys and now it is their turn, that of Mr. Nobilo, the Defence counsel of General Blaskic, to ask you questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Nuhagic, good afternoon. As you have heard, I am attorney Anto Nobilo, my colleague, Mr. Hayman. We will not keep you long, just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In January 1993, when HVO soldiers rounded up the men in your village, how many men were rounded up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Six, and I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were they all the men of the village, or were there more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, some men were in Maglaj on the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The persons you mentioned, Ivan Popovic, Akrap, were they neighbours, people living close by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the same local community that I belong to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So we can say that they lived close by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you reached Kaonik in January, were there any HVO Croatian soldiers detained there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you look into all the cells and all the buildings, all the premises, or were you just put in one cell and stayed there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in one cell, but when we went out to eat for meals, lunch or supper, I would see many cells.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you went to see a doctor because of your injuries, did anyone tell you that you may not tell the doctor how you were hurt, or was it your own decision out of fear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was out of fear, because I was afraid when I went back I would be treated even worse than I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In your cell, how many prisoners were detained there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is impossible to tell you when the number changes. They take some people out, bring new ones in, 17, 18, 20. Some people went off to dig and never returned, they spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was anyone beaten in your cell during their stay in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not from my cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How did the guards treat you in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They treated me correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did anyone hit you in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in Kaonik no one hit me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that some people were robbing the prisoners in Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you personally see any such robbery, that is the taking of jewellery, valuables et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was an HVO soldier who came to my cell and he took the boots of my colleague who was with me there in the cell, because he liked those boots, they were good boots.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was it a guard or someone from outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did he leave his own boots in exchange for the prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told him to clean them for him and to hand them back to the guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You spoke about some things that occurred when trenches were dug. You were not there, you did not go to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who it was that told you what had happened at trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was somebody called Mustafa Ibragic who died, who succumbed afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And who told you about the way in which Mustafa Ibragic died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My two nephews were in the same cell with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What are their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ramiz and Ekrem Nuhagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In January, how many days did you spend in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that I was taken into custody on 27th January, and in February, I do not recall the date, we were released.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were you in Kaonik one or two weeks or a month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About three weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Amongst you in Kaonik, were you all Muslim civilians or were there prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: A few words now about the April event. You said that they killed whoever they could, the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You described the death of five members of your family.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: With the exception of this truly tragic event, was anyone else killed in the village of Ocehnice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those five persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Apart from them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My uncle Ramiz was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And apart from that, was anyone else killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you see the members of your family die, or did you come across their bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I came across bodies burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And where had you left them before you found them after they were dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They stayed behind in a room on the ground floor which was used as dwelling space.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, when Amidja was wounded in the arm and went off with other inhabitants, how many people were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two cellars, two families, and they were in one where my uncle went, there were eight of them, and in the other cellar, there were two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you recognised people by their nicknames, the people who did those terrible things in your village, and then you mentioned several nicknames. Could you tell us the names, the first and last names of those people who did this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know their nicknames and I also know some of their full names.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Will you tell us then, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zarko Cosic, known as Cigo. Zeljo, Vujica, his surname is Vujica, Kologranic, known as Kole, Mlado, also Kologranic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was Ranko Kologranic there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, known as Kole.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And what about Zeljo Kologranic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mladen Kologranic as well, known as Madjo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was Jure Lovric there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him too, through the fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where did they live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: For example Zarko Cosic, where does he come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came -- he lives below my village, near the road. We knew each other, we would see each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And the Kologranics, where are they from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are from Carica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How far is that from your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please tell me, do you recall what Cosic Zarko said five days before the conflict to your sister Fatima? Could you repeat that to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can. He told my sister and neighbour, a woman neighbourhood prepared coffee for him and they were talking, and he said if any shooting should occur, and if any one member of his family were killed or wounded, that the village of Ocehnice would be burnt down and all of us would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did he say that he personally would torch the village of Ocehnice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did he do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was what was done, as it was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you went to the police station, do you know the building of the police station from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because it was during the communist system it was a police station too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, the investigators when they were interviewing you and asking you who set fire to the village, were they taking any notes? Did they write anything down about what they were asking you and what you were telling them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do remember they had a pen and paper in front of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And they wrote down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They wrote down my statement and my answers to their questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. How much time did you spend in the police station in Busovaca? How many hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember, but I stayed well into the night and I was taken there in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you stayed there until night-time, late into the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On several occasions, you said that these military policemen insisted that he should admit that they had done it. Who were you implying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many inhabitants did your village have before this tragic event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would need to take down a pen and recall the names and surnames and that would take a bit of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But just roughly, it does not have to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 18 to 20 members or families.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: 18 to 20 families or members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, please do not lose too much time on details. Try and go to the substance, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I will explain. I think that the police were carrying out an interrogation and the witness thought that he was the only survivor, but the police were aware that he was not and that the interrogation had another purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In that case, I will say that to you, as I have told the Prosecution, please ask the questions you want. Tell him, "we think that there were survivors from the village, do you agree or not?", but these multiple questions, round about questions are not necessary. The judges need the actual question you want to have answered, so please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It is a question of style. I am trying to extract the facts and let the court draw its own conclusions. It is a question of style. Was anyone watching over you in the village of Skradno? Were there guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were guards or rather a patrol that was walking around, HVO patrol.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly two at a time, they were patrolling and controlling.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there any wire round the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but we had nowhere to go anyway, because it was under the HVO control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did anyone attack you or disturb you in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They would come in, demand money. In the evening, they would come and ask for valuables to be given to them, to be loaded on to trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you complain to the patrol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What did they do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They said they could not do anything, apparently, because they could be exposed to threats by the soldiers that were out of control and that were better armed than they, so they did not dare oppose them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have you finished, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, do you have any clarifications, but related to the cross-examination only?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Mr. President. Mr. Nuhagic, you were asked some questions by Defence counsel about whether or not you saw your wife, mother and nieces and sister killed; do you remember those questions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. They were killed by a burst of fire, because my uncle told me he had seen it happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They were alive before the soldiers came into the village, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And they were dead after the soldiers left the village, were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And this attack and these murders was not carried out by Zarko Cosic alone, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President, thank you. Thank you, Mr. Nuhagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I should like to tell the witness, as I have announced earlier on, that the judges may have additional questions for him. Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nuhagic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would just like to clarify some of the information which your testimony has included. You mentioned that when you went out from the bus in Busovaca, a van came with a four barrel anti-aircraft and the crew dismounted and started beating you. The point is, you heard an argument among them about this beating, some were saying no and some were saying yes. Did in this argument, did they mention any orders coming from above which contained beating or which forbade beating, or was it just a debate, a friendly debate among them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They dismounted this vehicle on their own, and this vehicle had this anti-aircraft gun, so they did it on their own and started beating us. That is where I received the most blows.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, but I am asking about the discussion which you heard. Did these people beating you, did they mention that they had orders to beat you, or perhaps on the other hand those who were against beating you, did they say that the orders forbid beating? Either way, did any of them refer to orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You mentioned that there were very bad conditions when you were in jail. You had one toilet for 500 people. Where did these 500 people come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. From Busovaca, from the town itself, from the village of Skradno, the village of Krcevine, Podkula, the village of Loncari, from Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Speaking of Loncari by the way, you mentioned that Mirko Cosic, you heard him saying that they did a good job, that is what I noted down, that a good job was done in Loncari. Who was Mirko Cosic? Was he the head of any unit? What was he exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the commander of the unit called Jokers, which was a special purpose platoon or special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: He was a commander.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This "good job" meant what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He meant that Loncari, the people from Loncari had been expelled like I was, and that a number of people were killed there and even today no one knows about the whereabouts of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: When you spoke about the interrogation at the police station, where you had bloodstains on the walls and that sort, in this interrogation, you felt or you noticed that your investigator was astonished to know that there were still survivors from your village. Is that -- what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I meant by it that they were told at the police -- that is the soldiers who had come down from there, they told them that nobody had survived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The soldiers reported that the whole village was exterminated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Shahabuddeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Actually 11 people had survived, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Do you know whether the police interrogated any of those 11 survivors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I apologise, I did not have my headphone on at the time. You are living with a Croat person at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You are living in a Croat house at the moment, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How come you are living in a Croat house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was expelled from Busovaca, Busovaca is cleansed and the Croats left their own houses and their own properties and moved to Busovaca. Under what circumstances they left that, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let us talk a little about Mirko Cosic. You saw him on TV and Judge Riad asked you a question and you gave an answer. The Prosecutor had also asked you a question. He had asked you this question: was he an HVO soldier as well, and your answer to the Prosecutor was, "the commander of the unit called Jokers, who wore black uniforms and they were for special purpose unit". How should I understand your answer? Was he or was he not an HVO soldier as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a commander of the HVO unit called Jokers. He was in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I see, the Joker unit was a unit of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Got it. Then one last question. You remember that some HVO soldiers came up to you at one stage, some of them had masks, but you were able to identify some of them by their nicknames. Do you remember that evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where, at what location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think this was on 19th April at your village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I recognised them by their nicknames.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good. And some had masks on them, so you could not identify them by their faces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were you able to see any shoulder patches which they had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You could only see the HVO insignia on their arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: They had the HVO insignia on their arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We have almost completed. Was there any kind of particularly hostile attitude against you by the HVO? Were you part of the Territorial Defence or did you go on patrol? At the beginning of your narrative, in January 1993, you said, sometimes one gets the impression that people were looking specifically for you. Might you tell us very briefly or -- was it you specifically they were looking for, or was anybody who was Muslim being looked for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Any Muslim, all men from the village were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: A second question: there was no artillery fire which might have justified the impression, right or wrong, that the Draga barracks had been shelled from your village, that would have given them that impression? There were no reasons, no weapons, or were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You have gone through very painful experiences, you have been courageous in coming here. Ordinarily, you would have been a protected witness, but you said that you preferred not to be. You are now going to go home and we hope that one day your wounds will all have healed. Please do not move for the time being, the Tribunal will now suspend its sessions, the last of the week. We will begin to work again on Monday at 10.00. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: on Monday, 15th December 1997)
